lines.text: A benchmark's own average goes down after a change.
Does that genuinely mean every real user's own request got faster?
No, genuinely.
The real tail can genuinely move the opposite way.
Run it for real: a distribution's typical case and its real worst case are two genuinely separate numbers, read off the identical samples, not one number counted twice.
Now a real change is applied, and the real typical case genuinely drops.
Does the real worst case genuinely drop along with it?
No, genuinely.
The real worst case can genuinely rise instead.
Run it for real: the typical request genuinely got faster, while the real worst case genuinely got slower, from the identical change.
Now check the real average on this identical change.
Does it genuinely show the real worst case getting slower?
No, genuinely.
The average can genuinely improve while the tail genuinely regresses.
Run it for real: the real average genuinely improved too, completely hiding the real regression sitting in the tail.
Two real, independent sources on this exact discipline agree, in their own words.
A trustworthy measurement needs a real warmup and a real check for outliers first; an uncorrected sample can hide its own slowest requests entirely.

tolerated.line: A trustworthy measurement needs a real warmup and a real check for outliers first; an uncorrected sample can hide its own slowest requests entirely.

lines.text: So here's why a single number can never stand in for a benchmark's own result: an average is a statement about the bulk of a distribution, and the bulk is exactly where a real regression has the least room to hide.

The tail is the opposite case, a small share of requests that an average genuinely outvotes, which is exactly why a change that helps nearly everyone can still make the unluckiest request wait noticeably longer.

That's the real discipline underneath a trustworthy benchmark: treat the distribution as the real object being measured, and read its separate statistics separately, because the headline number was never standing in for all of them.
